David Chisnall (*Now with 50% more sarcasm!*) @david_chisnall
home original

The Free Software movement never escaped from its origins: the early ‘80s MIT AI Lab. Two things were true in this environment:

  • Back when most computers had tens of KiBs of RAM and 1 MiB was a huge amount, programs were simple. Very few programs were so complex that one person could not completely understand them.
  • The AI Lab was full of some of the most talented programmers in the world.

This meant that the only obstacles for these people being able to fix bugs and add features to any program were access to the source code and the legal rights to modify it. Once you have those, any program was understandable by that group and they could modify it however they wished.

For the next 40 years, the FSF focused on these two things. The world around them changed. These two prerequisites were never enough for most people (what do 90% of computer users do if you give them even a modest 10,000 line C codebase and tell them they can change it however they like?) and now they aren’t enough even for competent programmers.

When Linus says ‘fork it’ to folks who don’t want LLM-extruded code in their kernel, he knows full well that it is almost impossible to fork a 40 MLoC C (and Rust now) codebase that averages more than one CVE per day and have something useful.

The Free Software movement is struggling now because it obsessed over licenses, which was never a path that would succeed, and ignored the hard problems:

  • How do you design environments that enable end users to modify their software?
  • How do you engineer software so that it is cheap and easy for a random user to maintain a fork that meets their specific needs?
  • How do you foster communities where people want to share improvements, so forks don’t proliferate even when it’s easy?
  • How do you create an environment where everyone sees the benefits of user-modifiable code to such a degree that trying to sell anything that doesn’t come with these rights is commercially impossible?

Instead of tackling any of these problems, they created more complex and restrictive GPL variants. And well-paid lawyers found loopholes in them that allowed corporations to keep doing what they wanted (and even pick licenses like AGPLv3 to control ecosystems, because they give the copyright owners so many more rights than everyone else that it’s hard for anyone else to compete). They said ‘don’t worry about the complexity of the licenses, you only need to understand the legal details if you’re creating and distributing derived works’ while completely forgetting that making it possible for anyone to create and distribute modified versions of the programs was the entire point of the Free Software movement.

Multilinguo @multilinguo
home original

Did you know?

In Old Japanese, "papa" meant MOTHER.

Sound shift over 1000 years: p → f → h. Every papa became fafa, then haha 母.

Father evolved too: t → ch. Every titi became chichi 父.

Then in the 20th century, Japanese borrowed パパ and ママ from European languages. Now パパ means father.

Same syllables. Opposite parent. A thousand years apart.

#Etymology #Japanese #Linguistics #SoundChange

So here's my proposal for least convenient way of specifying a datetime:

- Japanese imperial year (eg Reiwa 8)
- Month and day in French Revolutionary calendar (eg Messidor 27)
- Time of day as Swatch .Beats (eg @760 )

Antifeatures of this system include:

- Can't predict future years "offline" (you need the realtime status of the Japanese royal family)
- Poor software support
- Intellectual property encumbrance (purely gratuitous because the First Republic had its own decimal time system)

I'm in one of those, a touch screen is the worst design ever made, moods. Why anyone in my generation accepted this and thought this was a good idea is beyond me.

For the sighted folks following me, a bit of a history.

In recent iOS upgrades for me there has been a vast disconnect between navigation and typing. When typing, keys just don't register, keys are slow to process, keys are just sluggish in general when typing on the virtual keyboard. It is madenning.

I hear it is the same on the Android side, so this isn't just an Apple thing.

Despite navigation being fine, still, I'd even argue that to sighted folk, sometimes, a touch interface just doesn't work.

I'm a pretty good typist but it took me thrice as long to compose one of my lengthy text messages asking a very important question, than when I used my PC to send an SMS message. Why did our generation believe typing on glass is cool. Nobody can type on glass.

I'm a very skilled typist and it takes me nearly 10 minutes to fiddle with the awful latency on the keyboard running VoiceOver. Navigating the phone is better, somewhat, but Apple fucked up typing speed forever I feel and I am not even sure what they did.

This is a problem with all mobile phones, I feel, not just Apple.

I've heard from sighted folks the virtual keyboard doesn't work for them either.
#UX #Apple #Rant #Rants

Stefano Marinelli @stefano

On 10 March 2021, I had only just fallen asleep when my phone started buzzing. Then another notification, and another. In a matter of minutes, 142 of my servers went up in the clouds. And not the cloud-computing kind.

Most of them were physically going up in a column of smoke in Strasbourg.

My wife looked at me and asked if I wanted a coffee. I nodded. It was going to be a very long day.

At EuroBSDCon 2026, I won't be giving a theoretical lecture on high availability. Instead, I’m going to tell the raw story of that night: the emergency recovery, the architectural choices that actually saved us, and the ones that crumbled under pressure (because we rarely talk about what fails).

Most of all, I’ll explain why that night changed my perspective, and why I’ve come to see BSD systems not just as operating systems, but as essential, practical tools for building simpler, more resilient infrastructure.

The official schedule is now live. If you want to hear a real-world post-mortem, join me on Saturday, 12 Sept at 11:15 (Room D.0.02).

My official AI policy for Schemacs Official AI Policy: “The Software Engineer’s Prime Directive“

I am borrowing the term, “The Prime Directive,” from the popular science fiction series Star Trek to describe my AI policy:

Every single line of code, every S-expression, every comment, every piece of documentation, every part of this software that serves a function must have that function be well-understood by at least one person (and of course, AI is not a person).

The term “well understood” is deliberately vague so that we (the Schemacs developer community) can decide on a case-by-case basis whether a person understands a function well enough.

Vibe coding is banned.

The definition of “Vibe Coding” is that you don’t bother to understand what the computer code means, if the software appears to behave in the way you expect you declare the code “correct.” By definition, vibe coding violates the Software Engineer’s Prime Directive.

Some LLM-generated output is OK.

If you suffer from some form of disability, and use an AI coding assistant to write code faster, this is perfectly acceptable so long you adhere to the Prime Directive — you must be able to defend the code you write by explaining the function of all of it’s component parts.

The term “disability” is deliberately vague because I don’t believe we as a community should define tests to decide whether someone qualifies as “having a disability.” If your disability is that you don’t like writing text, that is fine. Just obey the Prime Directive.

Unofficial AI Policy: we don’t need it.

This is a project for people to have fun. If you don’t like writing computer code, then don’t contribute computer code. There are plenty of other ways to contribute without needing AI coding.

There is no hurry, there is no deadline. Write code because you enjoy it, or because you want to learn how computers work. It is OK to take your time and enjoy yourself. There is really no reason to use AI for this project.

#tech #software #AI #LLMs #LLM #Scheme #R7RS #SchemeLang #Lisp #Schemacs #Emacs #EmacsLisp #Slop #VibeCoding #ClaudeCode #ChatGPT #SlopMachine

RE: https://raphus.social/@MaddieM4/116926325417565669

It's easy to think of Linux as a work product rather than a work process. You can point at a tarball full of source code or a git repository and say "that's Linux!" and you're not entirely wrong, but specifically through the lens of ongoing support, you're not adequately right. Linux is also the people who make the software. Linux is the regular patches that you need because Linux is too big to be complete or correct, and when some new vulnerability inevitably gets announced, a giant C codebase you don't have the skills to modify will not save you. It's distribution channels, it's funding. It's literal thousands of interpersonal trust relationships and unthinkable hours of free(ly contributed) labor. It is, compared to almost every other open source project or would-be development team, resource-infinite, while also a focal point of vendor lock-in for driver development.

"Those little white flowers you see here are known as the Arctic mountain heather, and they are highly toxic to this little pika.
Collared pika create what we call haypiles under the rocks that will serve as food for the 9 months of winter they endure beneath the snow. That’s 9 months of dead rotting plants for fungi, bacteria, and other parasites to completely destroy. That is, unless the pika layers toxic species like this arctic heather through the haypile.
This particular species of flower releases its toxic brew of phenolic compounds into the the pika's cache of food as it begins to break down. Those very same toxins, it turns out, are a natural food preservative that kills the very fungi and bacteria that would otherwise ruin an entire winter’s worth of food for the pika. And amazingly, by the time the pika makes it down to these layers, those toxins are completely harmless to the little mammal.
None of this is by accident. Researchers have documented that not only are pika meticulous at how they layer toxic plants into their haypiles, they use different species, with differing levels of toxicity, at specific levels through the cache to ensure that their food is not only well preserved but also timed to be edible for themselves as they work their way through it.
This is the most sophisticated pharmacological knowledge and behavior ever documented outside of humans."
photo and text by jaredlloydphoto

#Photographie #Photography #Fotografie #Nature #Wildlife #NaturePhotography #WildlifePhotography

Dear fedi people, maybe it’s the heat or the stress or Slop or the world itself, but the timeline is transforming into a twitter/X/F(ck)B like social meltdown, that is disproportionally negative and depressing. The planet still turns round.

Bad news and indignation and awareness to madness happening in the world are legitimate. But it’s okay to take a breath and think of the positive things around us, once we take our noses off the screens. The internet feeds on our despair at a time where we just need memes and some silly thoughts.

The slop, and gigallionaires and media can wait. They don’t deserve your immediate attention. They don’t deserve our permanent and continuous anger. Those who can’t rest can’t fight (and life shouldn’t be a permanent fight).

Spend some time with your loved ones, have sex, hug a tree, make music, invite your neighbour for an aperitivo, cook a meal… Read a book that has no triggers in it, or a dozen. It’s hard at first but worth it. Or chill for 1 hour.

Worst case scenario, if you really feel bad, find an old computer and set up a fresh Debian install. It will be a breeze and an opportunity to re-enjoy the wonders of compute. All problems will one “sudo apt” away from being solved.

If you play life in hard mode set up a BSD or Arch box… or build your own OS (depends on your orientations). The most important point is enjoying yourself… at the speed of your processor (if you are into this kind of shit).

#hugyourcomputer

fully remote (EU) #hiring #getfedihired #jembauche
it's that time again! it's time to #getfedihired (fully remote)
this one's a little unusual in that it's not for a specific position : in "theory" there would be 3 job postings; a python (web; django; postgres (to be reviewed)) developer, a devops (kubernetes, github actions (migrating off of)), and a cybersecurity compliance expert (knowledge base, setting up policies, dealing with audits...)

thing is though, there's definite overlap to these, and the priorities are different (there's no need for a full time cybersec person, for example)
on top of that, we prefer to hire people, not robots (derogatory, robots (endearing) are encouraged to apply) that perform a single task

so instead, we're hiring for people that have any or all of those skills
the way it'll work is we're gonna pick the best *combination* of 2-3 hires, rather than the best cybersec person we find, the best devops we find, etc : you may be surprised, but this gives most people reading this an advantage

the seniority levels are confirmed through principal, though salary ranges are only defined for confirmed and senior (40-48k for confirmed, 48-55k for senior; above that it's negotiable based on the specifics)
our definitions of seniority are not based on years of experience as well, but rather observed attitude and measured skillset (we make all of this public in the job offer)

main catch: you must have the right to work in France *before* applying (the company's managed to get a visa to someone before, but it was a disaster and upper management would rather not have to go through that again).
this doesn't mean right to *live* in France, just the right to hold a French contract (other types of contracts are also negotiable, no problem)
you must also be able to visit Paris or Grenoble as part of getting to know management, signing paperwork, etc (there's a story behind that one, but I'll only be sharing it to people I know)

if you're interested, DM me with any further questions, and I'll send you the job offer link with hints on how to get through very quickly
the goal is to have all 3 people picked and hired by the end of the month, which is roughly in line with how previous recruitment drives have gone with this company (in case you haven't applied to a job recently, that's roughly 10x faster than at the average employer; this is generally indicative of the internal state of the company : people-wise it's going pretty well)

#jembauche

If you know me, you know I've been ranting about how we should be able to prove injectivity of type constructors in a weak ambient logic. Or you've been challenged to prove it for MLTT with type-in-type. Or more recently you might have heard me yap about this really cool work by Thierry Coquand and Simon Huber that seemed to deliver some of that, but that I would have liked to understand because it looked rather magical.

Well here it is! Definitional inversion properties (injectivity + no-confusion of type constructors), via a domain theoretic model, in a weak ambient theory, and with type-in-type as a running example. And formalised thrice (!) for good measure.

I think this is a very useful technique that we have been in need of for a long time. With it denotational methods (syntax as initial model, etc) seem able to do things that were only possible with untyped confluence-based methods before. Domains are cool!

Also, with this line-up I feel like the obscure drummer of an incredible superband 😅

Mark Moxon @markmoxon
home original

Missiles are now working in two-player #BBCMicro Elite.

This clip shows player 1 firing a missile at player 2 (in the bottom view) and then player 2 retaliating (in both views).

This was really difficult to build! But it's important; here's why.

Until now, I've only had to draw the two ships, the planet and the sun.

There are shortcuts we can take for all of these: the sun and planet are so distant that we can ignore their orientations, and each ship is the origin of its own space view, which simplifies a lot of the maths.

Missiles, however, represent arbitrary objects in 3D space, so getting the maths working for them means we can add any objects to space and draw them from the perspective of any other objects.

So this means that multiplayer Econet Elite should be possible - mathematically, at least.

Nice!

#retrocomputing #retrogaming

Martin Escardo @MartinEscardo
home original

Claim. Formalization is an inherently informal activity.

Suppose you have done A informally on paper, and hopefully rigorously too, where A stands for Amazing Theorem.

Suppose further that you published A, after the reviewer(s) and the editor were satisfied with the rigour and the level of amazement.

Then you decide to formalize it, for whatever reason.

You do it, I claim *informally*, by sitting in front of a computer and typing things, which the proof assistant accepts and rejects successively in an interactive way, as so-called proof assistants work.

Or you give it for an LLM to do it faster while you drink coffee. It doesn't matter. My conclusion will be the same.

All the computer will check is what you typed in the keyboard.

It has no way of knowing whether you or the LLM actually formalized A or something else.

You have to check it (the LLM can't), and the checking is *inherently* informal.

And of course it has to be rigorous, too.

Wladimir Palant @WPalant
home original

I have been rethinking my life’s choices lately.

I’ve spent years building a knowledge base for Firefox extension developers. Despite all its flaws, and development complexity definitely was one of them, the Firefox extension ecosystem was meant to provide functionality that browser developers didn’t think about. Then Chrome came along and forced Mozilla to abandon its extensibility approach for one which was neatly limited to functionality that browser developers decided to allow. They had good technical reasons for that of course, but it replaced an ecosystem that embraced creativity by one which encourages endless repetitions of the same thing.

Now it’s educating people about security, another task I’ve spent years on. Currently this field is being killed by the so-called “AI.” Don’t get me wrong, I recognize the immense progress made on automated vulnerability finding. I see the short-term benefits. Yet the long-term outlook is grim. In a field that was already severely understaffed, this will result in even fewer people seriously learning about security. Yet the LLMs are by no means intelligent, nor will they ever be. They recombine existing human knowledge, and they are highly reliant on it. Without an influx of new knowledge their results will degrade.

Either way, I’m not complaining. It was fun while it lasted. But you probably shouldn’t expect new security research from me any time soon, I have little incentive to do it in this changed landscape.

Related to https://floss.social/@centricular/116919423714126703 I also want to expand a bit on LLM safety and censorship, which is only mentioned shortly there for practical purposes.

There's a lot of noise about that lately, and especially the big AI companies (Anthropic and OpenAI specifically) are painting a picture of advanced LLMs being too dangerous and that only they can be trusted with this power. Or otherwise cybercriminals or terrorists will use them to put an end to the civilized world. I'm sure they only argue like this with our best interests in mind.

On the other hand there's this report that terrorists are literally using ChatGPT and Claude: https://casp.ac/reports/ai-enabled-terrorism . So these companies are not actually preventing that and the only purpose seems to be to be to put themselves into the position of gatekeepers and pretend to care a lot about everybody's safety. I also don't think they possibly could prevent such usage. With enough motivation and resources you can get around every such obstacle.

Anyway, to the main topic.

- Sysadmins should have a seat at the table, not just have code thrown over the wall

Not everyone has someone to ask when they're stuck on their homework at 2am. I wanted to fix that, a math tutor that lives on your phone, works fully offline, and doesn't send your kid's schoolwork to anyone.

So I made LocalMathy! (My first mobile app, Android, iOS coming soon)

You get step-by-step help working through a typed out math problem. Or snap a photo of it if typing it out is annoying.

Its a small reasoning model that runs entirely on-device (about 2.1GB) because privacy shouldn't depend on trusting an API or AI company.. You can also bring your own model file instead of downloading mine!

(also, a model small enough to fit on my phone aced my entire uni math homework set while I was at the store buying brake pads. I don't think people know what's possible on-device yet. Because i also didn't know and was shocked)

Free and open source forever!

soon to be on f-droid!

but you can download now on github: https://github.com/micr0-dev/localmathy/releases

source: https://github.com/micr0-dev/localmathy

lmk if you hit bugs, still early days <3
